rv.q: First up, it’s not really a musical at all. There’s barely a new song in sight – instead, the score is an ingenious piecemeal of hits, from Whitney Houston to REM to Robyn.

Yet despite the meticulous replication, gone is the easy charm of the film, to be replaced by a slightly desperate air of forced jollity beneath the amply applied fake tan. In theory, it’s super-logical to turn a story that includes more than its fair share of camp flouncing about in tight sequinned costumes into a musical.

Baz Luhrmann’s divinely silly 1992 film about rebellion and repression in the frothy world of ballroom dance is a much-loved hit. When maverick Scott revolts against the rigid rules imposed by dance supremo Barry Fife (Gerard Horan), the latter smells revolution and stamps on the upstart as hard as a patent leather shoe will allow.
A dancing association president banging on about the rules becomes a Trump-like figure, and there’s a nonsense dream-sequence of political protest against him.

To create a great musical, all the stars in the creative firmament have to align: all the artistic and technical departments in a collaborative art-form involving, perhaps, a hundred people, have to coalesce as one.

Be careful what you sometimes wish for. When I reviewed this stage version of Baz Luhrmann's first hit film Strictly Ballroom from 1992 on its UK premiere at West Yorkshire Playhouse in late 2016, I praised the dancing - but wrote that it needs more work to resonate dramatically and scenically.
